Unit 8: The IA Cycle

SL curriculum overview and structured learning plan.

Introduction

How do we solve a real client's problem with code?

The Internal Assessment (IA) is your opportunity to behave like a professional developer. You will identify a client with a real problem, design a solution, build it using complex techniques, and evaluate its success. This is not just about coding — it's about the entire Cycle of Development.

You will follow the 5 Criteria: Planning (A) to define requirements, Design (B) to blueprint the system, Development (C) to prove your coding skills, Functionality (D) to demonstrate the product, and Evaluation (E) to reflect on the outcome.

Criterion A: Planning

Everything starts with a Problem Specification. You must:

  • Identify a real Client (Stakeholder).
  • Define the scenario and why a digital solution is needed.
  • List specific, measurable Success Criteria (e.g., "The system shall calculate averages in under 2 seconds").
Criterion B: Solution Overview

Before coding, you plan. This criterion covers:

  • Record of Tasks: A chronology of your work (e.g., a GANTT chart).
  • Design Overview: Flowcharts, UML diagrams, and UI wireframes that blueprint your solution.
Criterion C: Development

This is the "Complexity" criterion. You must demonstrate high-level coding skills (e.g., Sorting, Searching, File I/O, OOP) and document how you implemented them. It's not about the whole code, but the ingenious parts.

Criterion D: Functionality

Does it work? You will produce a Video (max 7 minutes) demonstrating the features defined in Criterion A. The examiner assesses the product based on this video.

Key Terminology
TermDefinition
Internal Assessment (IA) A significant project (20% of grade) where students develop a software solution for a client.
Stakeholder (Client) The person who will use the product. You must consult them throughout the process.
Success Criteria A list of specific, measurable requirements that the final product must meet.
Record of Tasks A chronological list (often a GANTT chart) showing the planning, design, dev, and testing stages.
Prototype An early model of the product used to get feedback from the client.
Complexity The level of technical difficulty in the code (e.g., using nested loops, custom classes, or recursion).
Evaluation Critically assessing whether the solution met the success criteria and suggesting future improvements.

Syllabus Coverage

  • Crit A Planning & Requirements
  • Crit B Design & Record of Tasks
  • Crit C Development (Complexity)
  • Crit D Functionality (Video)
  • Crit E Evaluation

Applications

  • Inventory systems for local shops
  • Scheduling tools for schools
  • Educational games for primary students
  • Data visualization for science labs
  • Club membership management
